buckets.title: Motion in a Plane (CBSE Class XI, Unit II Kinematics) with labelled JEE extensions
buckets.badge_reason: Learners must move between vector algebra and plane kinematics while keeping one frame, one clock and each model's validity conditions in view.

curriculum_mappings.locator: Class XI Theory, Unit II Kinematics, Chapter 3 Motion in a Plane

conventions.statement: Declare one x-y frame (origin and axis directions) before writing any component; every component of one problem uses that frame.
i-hat and j-hat are unit vectors along the declared x and y axes.

scope.covers: Scalars and vectors, equality, multiplication by a real number, graphical and analytical addition and subtraction, resolution into rectangular components, motion in a plane with constant acceleration, projectile motion and uniform circular motion, as listed by the CBSE 2026-27 curriculum and the NCERT chapter; five JEE extension microtopics are carried as labelled extensions.

capabilities.action: Classify a physical quantity as scalar or vector, draw a displacement from its end points alone, and judge whether two vectors are equal.
capabilities.success_criterion: Names direction as the deciding property, gives the same displacement for every path between fixed end points, separates path length from displacement magnitude, and calls two vectors equal only when magnitude and direction both match.

curriculum_mappings.locator: Class XI Unit II Chapter 3: scalar and vector quantities; position and displacement vectors; equality of vectors

microtopics.title: Scalars and vectors; position and displacement vectors; equality of vectors
microtopics.badge_reason: Each idea is a single definition, but learners carry over the everyday habit of reading distance travelled as displacement, which the first exercises are built to expose.
entry_assumptions: Can measure a length and state a direction such as east or 30 degrees from a reference line.
Can mark a point on a grid relative to a chosen origin.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Because a vector carries a direction as well as a magnitude, the displacement between two positions is fixed by the end points alone, so it differs from the path length whenever the object changes direction.

teaching_path.action: Sort quantities into scalars, which have magnitude only, and vectors, which have magnitude and direction and add by the triangle (or parallelogram) law.
teaching_path.why_valid: These are the textbook definitions every later vector operation relies on.
teaching_path.output: two labelled lists: magnitude-only quantities and magnitude-plus-direction quantities

teaching_path.action: Fix a reference point as origin so each position of the object can be drawn as an arrow from it.
teaching_path.why_valid: A displacement is read off two positions, so both positions must be located from one agreed point.
teaching_path.output: origin O with the initial position P and final position Q marked

teaching_path.action: Draw the displacement as the single straight arrow from P to Q and check it against several different routes from P to Q.
teaching_path.why_valid: The displacement vector joins the initial and final positions and does not depend on the path actually taken between them.
teaching_path.output: one arrow PQ shared by every route, such as PABCQ, PDQ and PBEFQ

teaching_path.action: Compare each route's path length with the length of arrow PQ.
teaching_path.why_valid: Path length equals the displacement magnitude only if the object never changes direction; in all other cases the path length is greater.
teaching_path.output: path length >= |PQ|, with equality only for the straight route

teaching_path.action: Test two arrows for equality by comparing both magnitude and direction, sliding one parallel to itself onto the other if needed.
teaching_path.why_valid: Two vectors are equal if and only if magnitude and direction match; free vectors may be shifted parallel to themselves, but a vector whose line of application matters may not.
teaching_path.output: equal or not equal, with the failing property named

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Path length and the magnitude of displacement are the same quantity.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A runner completes exactly one lap of a closed track and stops at the start line. What are the path length and the magnitude of the displacement?
misconceptions.repair: Displacement depends only on the end points, which coincide here, so it is zero; the path length is the whole lap. The two agree only when the motion never changes direction.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Two arrows of the same length are equal vectors.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: One displacement is 5 m east and another is 5 m north. Are they equal vectors?
misconceptions.repair: No. Equality needs the same magnitude and the same direction; these share only the magnitude.

exit_task.prompt: A student walks 30 m east and then 40 m north. Without calculating, say whether the magnitude of the displacement is less than, equal to or greater than the 70 m walked, and name what fixes the displacement.

answer.summary: Less than 70 m, because the student changed direction; the displacement is fixed only by the start and end points.
reasoning: The path turns through a corner, so the path length exceeds the displacement magnitude.
The displacement is the straight arrow from the start point to the end point, whatever route joins them.
answer.check: A straight walk to the same end point would have a path length equal to the displacement magnitude.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer compares two lengths qualitatively and states no computed value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Anchors the scalar/vector split and the path independence of displacement to verified NCERT text so that the vector-algebra microtopics can build on them.

representations.purpose: Show several different routes between the same initial and final positions next to the one straight displacement arrow they share, so path length and displacement are seen as different quantities.
required_elements: at least two distinct routes from P to Q
single displacement arrow from P to Q
read_order: single displacement arrow from P to Q
at least two distinct routes from P to Q
instance_constraints: Every route starts at P and ends at Q.
Exactly one displacement arrow is drawn, straight, with its head at Q.
Any route drawn straight along PQ is labelled with a path length equal to |PQ|; every bent route has a longer label.
accessibility: Each route is identified by a text label, not colour alone.
The displacement arrow's direction is stated in words as from P to Q.
misleading_alternatives: Drawing a separate displacement arrow along each route.
Labelling the displacement with the length of a curved route.

correspondence.element: single displacement arrow from P to Q
correspondence.in_words: The change of position, fixed by the two end points only.
The distance actually travelled along that route.

question_families.title: Scalar/vector classification and displacement versus path length
solution_structure: Decide whether the quantity needs a direction to be specified.
Locate the initial and final positions and draw the straight displacement between them.
Compare the displacement with the path actually travelled, and divide by the elapsed time only after choosing which one the question asks for.

demand_dimensions.model_choice: Choose between the path-length reading and the displacement reading of how far an object went.
demand_dimensions.representation_translation: Turn a verbal route or a figure into two marked end points and one arrow.
demand_dimensions.reasoning_steps: Identify the end points, find the straight-line separation, compare with the route length, then form rates if asked.
demand_dimensions.novelty: Routes vary from straight lines to arcs and detours while the end points stay fixed.

safe_variations: Change the route between fixed end points.
Change the list of quantities to classify, keeping the magnitude-only versus magnitude-and-direction test.
transfer_boundaries: Do not treat a closed route's path length as its displacement.
Do not shift a vector whose line of application matters when testing equality.
common_wrong_routes: Report the route length as the displacement.
Call speed and velocity the same quantity because they share units.

questions.stem: State, for each of the following physical quantities, if it is a scalar or a vector : volume, mass, speed, acceleration, density, number of moles, velocity, angular frequency, displacement, angular velocity.
conditions: Use the textbook definitions: a scalar has magnitude only; a vector has magnitude and direction and obeys the triangle law of addition.

answer.summary: Scalars: volume, mass, speed, density, number of moles, angular frequency. Vectors: acceleration, velocity, displacement, angular velocity.
reasoning: For each quantity ask whether stating it fully requires a direction.
Volume, mass, density and number of moles are complete as a number with a unit.
Speed and angular frequency are magnitudes only, while velocity, acceleration, displacement and angular velocity carry a direction.
This matches the official key: the six listed quantities are scalars and the rest are vectors.
answer.check: Every vector in the list has a scalar partner or a direction attached; no quantity is left unclassified.

reasoning_route.action: Rewrite each quantity as the question 'does specifying it need a direction?'.
reasoning_route.why_valid: The definitions separate scalars from vectors by direction alone.

reasoning_route.action: Split look-alike pairs: speed versus velocity, angular frequency versus angular velocity.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Paired quantities share units, so only the direction test separates them.
reasoning_route.output: speed and angular frequency scalar; velocity and angular velocity vector

reasoning_route.action: Count the classes against the list of ten.
reasoning_route.why_valid: A complete answer places every listed quantity exactly once.

scaffolds.text: For each quantity, try to state it completely without a direction. If you cannot, it is a vector.

extensions.grade9v3:figure_note: NCERT Fig. 3.19 shows the three skaters' routes from P to Q; read it on the cited page.

questions.stem: Three girls skating on a circular ice ground of radius 200 m start from a point P on the edge of the ground and reach a point Q diametrically opposite to P following different paths as shown in Fig. 3.19. What is the magnitude of the displacement vector for each ? For which girl is this equal to the actual length of path skate ?
conditions: The ground is a circle of radius 200 m and Q is diametrically opposite P.
Displacement depends only on the initial and final positions.

answer.summary: The displacement has magnitude 400 m for each girl; it equals the path length only for girl B.
reasoning: All three start at P and finish at Q, so they share one displacement vector PQ.
PQ is a diameter: 2 x 200 m = 400 m.
Path length equals displacement magnitude only for a route that never changes direction, which the key identifies as girl B's.
answer.check: The displacement cannot exceed any route's length, and 400 m is the shortest distance across the circle.

reasoning_route.action: Mark P and Q and draw one straight arrow PQ across the circle.
reasoning_route.why_valid: The displacement joins the end points and ignores the routes.
A diameter is twice the radius.

reasoning_route.action: Pick the route whose length equals |PQ|.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Only a route with no change of direction has path length equal to displacement magnitude.

scaffolds.text: Ignore the routes for a moment: where does each girl start and where does she finish?

questions.stem: A passenger arriving in a new town wishes to go from the station to a hotel located 10 km away on a straight road from the station. A dishonest cabman takes him along a circuitous path 23 km long and reaches the hotel in 28 min. What is (a) the average speed of the taxi, (b) the magnitude of average velocity ? Are the two equal ?
conditions: Station-to-hotel straight-line distance 10 km, path length 23 km, elapsed time 28 min.

answer.summary: (a) 49.3 km/h; (b) 21.4 km/h. They are not equal, because average speed equals the magnitude of average velocity only for a straight path.
reasoning: Convert the time: 28 min = 28/60 h = 0.467 h.
Average speed uses the path length: 23 km / 0.467 h = 49.3 km/h.
Average velocity uses the displacement: 10 km / 0.467 h = 21.4 km/h.
The route was circuitous, so path length exceeds displacement and the two rates differ.
answer.check: Average speed is at least the magnitude of average velocity, and 49.3 > 21.4 agrees.

reasoning_route.action: Assign 23 km to the speed and 10 km to the velocity.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Average speed divides path length by time; average velocity divides displacement by time.
reasoning_route.output: speed uses 23 km, velocity uses 10 km

reasoning_route.action: Divide each distance by the time in hours.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Both rates share the one elapsed time.
They coincide only when the path is straight.

scaffolds.text: Which of the two distances, 23 km or 10 km, is a displacement?
